title: School Notebooks 5-pack

drivers.name: TikTok trend (new driver, no past data)
drivers.evidence: Product trending on TikTok with no prior occurrence; noise-adjusted promotion lift from past is only x1.16; recent higher price weeks show no lift; evidence is thin, so effect shrunk.

drivers.name: Price increase (2.3%)
drivers.evidence: Price rose to $9.03; recent weeks at this price show 7–10 units, below baseline; price increases reduce demand; effect is moderate but supported by recent data.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 7.7. No events or promotions are scheduled. The price increased 2.3% to $9.03, which may dampen demand. The product is trending on TikTok, a novel driver with no past data. The classical uplift model suggests no effect, but this ignores the viral trend. Recent weeks show no lift at the higher price, and the 30% off promotion in April had a strong lift (x2.86), but that was a deeper discount. The TikTok trend is untested; evidence is thin. We shrink the effect toward 1.0. The noise-adjusted estimate for past promotions is only x1.16, and the recent higher price weeks show no lift. The trend is likely to be modest and uncertain.

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 9.03 (+2.3% vs regular price 8.83)
  planner notes: Product is trending on TikTok

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 7.7 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 33.1 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 21.9

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-64% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
